page.title: Build a team chat with tinyactors
page.description: Try a team chat in your browser, then build it in nine steps, from one room to direct messages between two people.

hero.headline: Build a team chat
hero.lede: Try the finished chat in this tab, then build it in nine steps, each a program you can run.

section.heading: Chat as any of six people
section.p: Each person and channel is an actor in this tab, and you are forager: switch person from your avatar's menu. The debugger at the top right cuts a person's connection or switches the running chat between steps 5 and 9.

playground.description: A team chat, The Hill, with channels, direct messages and six people, each an actor; you are forager, and your avatar's menu signs you out or switches person. Its debugger runs the simulated clock, loses a person's connection, makes a screen drop or delay messages, runs scenarios, shows each actor's chart in its current state and a log, and moves the running chat between the tutorial's steps 5 and 9 by live migration.

section.heading: 1. Create a room
section.p: A room is an actor with a list of members: join adds to it, and post sends to all of them. The text leaves the chart as a message to chat:client, which your program handles.
Here a Client prints what each member's screen would show. The program starts a room and sends it two joins and a post.

section.heading: 2. Track who is online
section.p: A user who stops typing sends no event, so nothing marks them away. The user's chart restarts a 300-second timer on each activity, and when it fires, the chart moves to away.
The room now sends each post to each member's user actor, by its name. A user who is offline ignores it.
A simulated clock moves 300 seconds in no time, so the program sees both users go away.

section.heading: 3. Create each room once
section.p: Two users who create general at the same moment could get two rooms. One workspace actor creates every room with a spawn send and records the name at once, so a repeat is refused.
A user joins a room by its name. A join sent to a room that does not exist comes back to the user as error.communication.
With actor.ask, the program requests general twice and two invalid names; then bob joins a room that does not exist.

section.heading: 4. Show everyone who is online
section.p: A user who connects late has missed every status change made before. Each user now reports its status to the workspace, which keeps them all.
A newcomer gets the whole roster, and each user online gets every change after that.

section.heading: 5. Keep idle users out of memory
section.p: Most users sit idle, yet each one's actor stays in memory. Give the host a store and a resident bound, and actors past the bound wait in the store.
The charts are step 4's: an event, or a user's 300-second timer, loads a saved actor again.

section.heading: 6. Show who is typing
section.p: A notice for every key would flood every screen. The user's chart tells its room at most once every 3 seconds, on a timer of its own.
Each other member's chart shows the notice for 5 seconds after the last one, restarting its timer on each.
A post takes the typist's notice off every screen, so it ends the typist's 3 seconds too. The first key after a post is told at once.
When its user disconnects, the chart cancels its timers and takes each notice off the user's screen.
Ada's three keys make one notice, and bob's notice runs out by itself. Cat's disconnect takes bob's notice off cat's screen, and ada's key right after a post shows at once.

section.heading: 7. Ride out a lost connection
section.p: A phone in a tunnel loses its connection for a few seconds, and until now its user went offline at once. Now the user's chart reports away, as Slack shows it, and keeps new messages for 30 seconds in reconnecting.

Back within 30 seconds, the history state resume returns the user to active or away, whose entry reports that status again. The held messages reach the screen, and the raised reconnected asks the workspace for the roster once the status is out.
Ada sees bob away, then active 10 seconds later; he gets the held message and a roster with cy offline. Then he is gone for 40 seconds: only the second loss makes him offline.

section.heading: 8. Show a room's history to late joiners
section.p: A member who joins late saw nothing said before, and a member who joined twice got every post twice. A channel's history is data your program stores; the room sends each post to the store, which numbers and times it.
The store is an I/O processor of your program. It numbers and times each post, so a screen shows when it was posted, however late it arrives.
A join adds the member only once, and answers joined so the screen reads the store.
A member who signs out misses the posts made meanwhile: the room sends them, but an offline user drops them. When the connection opens, the screen reads what it lacks from the store.

Cat joins after two posts and reads both; bob joins a second time, and the third post reaches him once. Cat signs out for the fourth post and reads it five minutes later, stamped with the time bob posted it.

section.heading: 9. Send a direct message
section.p: Two people who want to talk privately have only channels, which anyone can join. A direct message is a room of the two, which the workspace makes once per pair.
Either side asks for dm.forager.scout: the two names, sorted. A channel's name holds no dot, so no channel takes it.
The room chart builds on step 8's, so a direct message keeps history, typing and catch-up. Its members come with the spawn, and the room refuses anyone else's join.

The other person hears of their direct messages from the workspace when they come online, as they hear the roster. Back from a lost connection, the user chart asks for them with dms.get, as it asks roster.get.
Scout writes to forager, who is signed out and reads both posts on signing in. Queen's join is refused, and her post reaches nobody.

section.heading: Take it to production
section.p: The charts stay as they are; what changes is what your program connects them to.

item.text: Here a screen is a list in memory. In production, chat:client writes to each user's socket, and a closed socket sends disconnect.
Step 5's store forgets everything when the process ends. SQLiteStore keeps saved actors on disk.
A new chart leaves running users on the old one. New users start on the new chart, and a migration moves the running ones.
A slow post could be waiting in any of its actors. Every step is a span, so the trace shows where it waited.
